title: Blue carbon

definition.text: Carbon taken up and stored by living marine systems, especially coastal ones, in ways that people can manage.

facts.text: Most often the term means the carbon captured by tidal marshes, mangroves and seagrass meadows.
These vegetated coastal ecosystems bury carbon fast because they pile it up in their soils and sediments.
Coastal sediments lack oxygen, so organic carbon in them can be preserved for decades to millennia, far longer than most land carbon stocks.
When blue carbon ecosystems are damaged or lost, they release their carbon back to the air and add to greenhouse gas emissions.
Managing them counts as an ocean-based biological form of carbon dioxide removal, and can serve both climate mitigation and ecosystem-based adaptation.
The term was coined in 2009 to stress that coastal vegetated ecosystems contribute far more than their share to global carbon sequestration.
Seagrass, salt marshes and mangroves are sometimes called 'blue forests', in contrast to green forests on land.

contested_note: Sources say the long-term effectiveness of blue carbon as a carbon dioxide removal method is still under debate.

verification.title: Dimensions of Blue Carbon and emerging perspectives

definition.text: Tidal marshes are intertidal ecosystems of non-woody plants that act as important carbon sinks.

facts.text: Marshes lock carbon in their roots and buried plant matter because sediment builds up fast and decomposition happens largely without oxygen.
Much of their production is belowground, and these deposits can be up to 8 m deep.
Salt marshes cover roughly 22,000 to 400,000 km2 worldwide and bury an estimated 210 g C m−2 yr−1.
They also shelter birds and young fish, protect coasts from storm surge and flooding, and cut nutrient loads reaching coastal waters.

definition.text: Seagrass meadows bury a large share of ocean carbon in their sediments despite covering a tiny part of the sea floor.

facts.text: Seagrass covers only 0.1% of the ocean floor but accounts for roughly 10–18% of total oceanic carbon burial.
Global seagrass meadows may store as much as 19.9 Pg of organic carbon.
Burial rates vary with species, sediment and depth, averaging about 138 g C m−2 yr−1.

conflicts.text: Seagrass covers about one percent of the sea floor and may deliver 15–18% of ocean carbon storage.
conflicts.note: Sea rewilding gives about 1% of sea-floor area and 15–18%, against 0.1% and 10–18% on Blue carbon.

definition.text: Carbon stored in deep ocean waters and the sea floor of the high seas, beyond national jurisdictions.

facts.text: It covers carbon in continental shelf waters, deep-sea waters and the sea floor beneath them, and makes up 90% of all ocean carbon.
It is seen as less amenable to management because data on how permanent these stores are is lacking.
Below about 3 km, CO2 becomes liquid and sinks to the seafloor because it is denser than the seawater around it.
Techniques being explored include seaweed farming, ocean fertilization, artificial upwelling and basalt storage.

title: Seaweed as blue carbon

definition.text: The open question of whether seaweed (macroalgae) forests should count as blue carbon ecosystems.

facts.text: Seaweed forests are strong candidates because they are highly productive and cover coasts worldwide.
A 2016 report estimated they could sequester 173 TgC per year (range 61–268), but the estimate is very uncertain.
Their carbon can be stored by burial in nearby sediments, export to the deep ocean, or as dissolved organic carbon that resists breakdown.
Tracking where seaweed carbon ends up is very hard, so precise estimates of their sequestration capacity are lacking.

contested_note: Sources call it contentious whether macroalgae count as blue carbon ecosystems, since their long-term carbon storage is unproven.

title: Managed retreat

definition.text: The planned, coordinated movement of people, buildings and infrastructure away from places at risk.

facts.text: It can respond to many hazards, including floods, wildfire and drought.
Sea level rise from climate change is drawing attention from politicians, insurers and residents to retreat from low-lying coasts.
Its form depends on the location, the type of hazard and local policies.
Some low-lying countries facing flooding, such as Kiribati, are planning to relocate their populations.
Managed retreat can be very controversial, yet more communities consider it as the costs of adaptation rise.
One New Zealand coastal hazards expert argues retreat is mainly a social and political issue rather than a technical one.
Retreating from high-risk areas such as floodplains reduces exposure.
Whether migration counts as adaptation is debated; the IPCC says it may or may not.

contested_note: Retreat programs have met lawsuits and resistance from residents worried about home values and insurance costs.
distinct_from: Adaptation costs and the adaptation gap

definition.text: Deliberately removing or breaching coastal flood defences so the sea can reclaim land and form natural soft landforms such as salt marsh.

facts.text: In the UK its main aim is coastal stability, replacing hard defences with natural soft landforms.
Its big drawback is that land must be given up to the sea, but the new natural areas buffer land further inland by absorbing water and damping waves.
It is also used to make up for lost intertidal habitat such as salt marsh lost to erosion and coastal squeeze.
At Abbott's Hall Farm in Essex, five breaches in an old sea wall let the sea create nearly 280 hectares of salt marsh.
Few sites are monitored consistently, so results have been very unpredictable.

definition.text: Programs in which government buys at-risk properties and relocates or demolishes them, a form of managed retreat.

facts.text: Relocation has been used inland and on coasts after severe flooding and hurricanes.
Sometimes single homes are bought after disasters; sometimes whole communities move, as at Valmeyer, Illinois, or Isle de Jean Charles, Louisiana.

definition.text: Rehabilitating degraded or destroyed mangrove forests so they return to a state like their condition before disturbance.

facts.text: Mangroves provide water filtration, fish nurseries, medicines, food and timber, and protect coasts from erosion and storm surges.
Mangroves store three to four times more carbon than other tropical forests.
Simply planting single-species stands in places thought suitable usually fails, because the soil and water needs of mangroves are not met.
Better methods let damaged areas regrow naturally by secondary succession, provided tidal and freshwater flows work and seedlings are available.
Mangroves are seen as one of the easiest coastal systems to restore because seedlings can survive where no adult trees remain.
Successful restoration would need an estimated US$0.3–1.6 billion per year until 2050; debt-for-nature swaps have been proposed to help pay.
Long-term success depends on support and participation of local communities.
Mangroves provide water filtration, nurseries for aquatic life, medicinal materials, food and timber.

definition.text: The rapid worldwide decline of mangrove forests, driven by clearing for development, aquaculture and farming and by climate change.

facts.text: Mangroves are being lost faster than inland tropical rainforests.
At least 35% of global mangrove area has been lost, and the decline continues at 1-2% per year.
Mangroves make up only 0.7% of tropical forest area but their clearing contributes 10% of global CO2 emissions from deforestation.
Whether a mangrove forest survives sea level rise depends on whether its sediment builds up as fast as the sea rises.

definition.text: Involving local communities in planning, doing and maintaining mangrove restoration.

facts.text: Projects without community support risk backlash and wasted money and effort.
Valuing restoration is hard because most mangrove services are indirect and not sold in markets.
Locals add knowledge of the environment, and paid work and funding give them reason to keep maintaining the mangroves.

title: REDD+ and mangroves
article: Mangrove restoration#Reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation

definition.text: Using the UN REDD+ mechanism, which pays developing-country stakeholders to avoid deforestation, to protect and restore mangroves.

facts.text: The UN launched the REDD program in 2008 to cut emissions and strengthen forest carbon sinks.
In Thailand, carbon markets pay farmers to keep mangroves by making up for the income they forgo from shrimp farming.

definition.text: Natural and human-led processes for restoring damaged coral reefs.

facts.text: Reefs host over 25% of marine life, buffer coasts from storms and erosion, and support food, jobs and tourism for coastal communities.
Half the world's coral has disappeared since 1970.
The usual method is to break mature corals into fragments, grow them on lines or supports, and transplant them to the reef once large enough.
Restoration has grown in prominence because of unprecedented reef die-offs around the planet.
Coral gardening may not save every species; instead it can help natural recovery and widen a species' genetic pool.
Propagated corals raise the worry that some may spread like invasive species and harm biodiversity.

definition.text: Cultivating coral by growing small fragments in nurseries until mature, then moving them to damaged reefs.

facts.text: A wild colony is cut into smaller pieces, which grow asexually into new colonies genetically identical to the parent.
Ocean-based nurseries hang fragments on lines or fix them to structures; land-based nurseries grow them in tanks.
Fragmentation gives about an 8x increase in colony growth compared with the donor coral.
Most colonies grow only about an inch a year, and land tanks shield them from storms, predators and disease.

definition.text: A coral-growing technique that cuts live coral into very small pieces which, fixed to plugs in tanks, grow much faster.

facts.text: It was developed by David Vaughan in 2006 and relies on coral's ability to clone itself.
It speeds up the growth of reef-building corals from years to, often, months.

definition.text: Repairing and rebuilding degraded oyster reefs.

facts.text: By 2011 an estimated 85% of the world's oyster reefs had been lost to over-harvesting, destructive fishing, pollution and disease.
Projects aim for a working three-dimensional reef that supports biodiversity, protects shorelines, traps sediment and cleans water.
Sites are chosen by surveys of salinity, water quality, past reefs, substrate, disease, predators and other factors.
Restored reefs can recover oyster densities to match healthy natural reefs.
Cleaner water from healthy oysters benefits commercial and recreational fishing, boating and ecotourism, and projects create and safeguard jobs.
Introducing non-native oyster species to a new habitat can do more harm than good.

definition.text: Laying down cultch, such as old shell or similar hard material, to give young oysters surfaces to settle on and rebuild a reef.

facts.text: Oyster larvae swim freely for about three weeks, then must attach to a hard surface to become spat.
Used oyster and clam shells from farmers and restaurants are cleaned and returned to the water as settling surfaces.
Cultching, pioneered for oyster farming in the early 19th century, has been the most successful way to reform oyster beds.

definition.text: Defending coasts against flooding and erosion, including techniques that stop erosion to claim land.

facts.text: Coastal zones cover less than 15% of Earth's land yet host more than 40% of the world's people.
Nearly 1.2 billion people live within 100 km of a coastline and 100 m of sea level.
Protection matters more as climate change speeds up sea level rise in the 21st century.
Before the 1950s the norm was hard structures such as seawalls, revetments and groynes.
From the late 1940s, cost and ugliness pushed engineers toward artificial beaches and stabilized dunes that copy natural protection.
Measures often worked locally but made problems worse elsewhere, sometimes tens of kilometres away.

definition.text: The broad choices for responding to coastal change: abandon, retreat, armour, build seaward, or raise land and buildings.

facts.text: The five generic strategies are abandonment, managed retreat or realignment, armouring with hard structures, building defences seaward, and elevating land and buildings.
The choice depends on local sea-level change, landforms, sediment supply and erosion, plus social, economic and political factors.
Integrated coastal zone management can instead keep development out of erosion- or flood-prone areas.
Moving seaward can create valuable new land but leaves developed coasts open to coastal squeeze.
Limited intervention, used where land has little economic value, lets salt marshes and dunes develop and absorb wave energy.

definition.text: A coastal strategy that keeps the shoreline where it is, usually by hardening it with permanent concrete and rock structures.

facts.text: Seawalls, groynes, detached breakwaters and revetments make up more than 70% of protected shorelines in Europe.
Soft options such as beach nourishment and dune stabilization can also hold the line by working with natural processes.
Armouring often just moves the problem to another stretch of coast, and maintenance costs can eventually force a change of strategy.

definition.text: A wall or barrier built at right angles to the coast to trap sand carried along the shore and so build up a beach.

facts.text: Sand piles up on one side, widening the beach, but beach material is lost on the other side.
Groynes are cheap, need little maintenance and are among the most common defences, though many communities oppose their look.
The last groyne in a series stops sand from reaching beaches further along, a problem called terminal groyne syndrome.

definition.text: Recording where the shoreline is and how it moves over time, a basic need for coastal scientists, engineers and managers.

facts.text: Defining the shoreline is hard because coasts are dynamic and tides shift its position at any moment.
Data come from historical maps, aerial photographs used since the 1920s, beach profiling surveys, remote sensing and video.
Monitoring campaigns show past shoreline movement and support predictions of future change.

definition.text: A way of protecting shorelines and marshes from erosion that uses as many natural elements as possible instead of walls.

facts.text: Unlike bulkheads and seawalls, which worsen erosion, living shorelines buffer wave energy more effectively.
Building one is a form of soft engineering, applying ecological principles to shoreline stabilization.
Common materials include sand, wetland plants, oyster reefs, submerged aquatic vegetation, stones and coir fibre logs.
Benefits include filtering runoff, creating habitat, absorbing wave energy and supporting fisheries, possibly at lower cost than seawalls.
Projects move through site analysis, permitting, site preparation, installation, then maintenance and monitoring.
Low rock sills or breakwaters seeded with oyster spat calm the water so marsh grasses can be planted behind them.

definition.text: A coastal management practice that keeps sand dunes from eroding.

facts.text: Dunes protect inland areas from storms, waves and seawater, and can resupply eroded beaches with sand.
They also give habitat to specialized plants and animals, including rare and endangered species.
Stabilizing them combines planting vegetation against wind and water, wooden sand fences that hold sand, and footpaths that keep walkers off.
Vegetation binds the sand; without it, wind moves sand inland in a process called sand encroachment.
In about 30 years, nearly 75% of the Mediterranean's coastal dunes were damaged or destroyed, mainly by tourism.
Dune management counts as a soft technique, unlike hard defences whose end effects cause erosion on neighbouring coasts.
Without public understanding and support, coastal dune management is virtually impossible.

definition.text: The bands of plants across a beach dune, from the sea-facing foredune through the backdune to a later shrub stage.

facts.text: Foredune plants must tolerate salt spray, strong winds and burial by blowing sand.
On the dune plain and backdune, plants grow into dense 'dune mats' that hold the dune together.
Once these herbaceous plants are established, deeper-rooted shrubs can follow, and the shrub stage may eventually give way to forest or chaparral.
In New Zealand, introduced marram grass built steep, storm-vulnerable dunes and crowded out native plants; it is now classed as a pest.

title: Climate-driven community relocation
article: List of areas depopulated due to climate change

definition.text: Whole or partial abandonment of places, or plans to move their people, because of human-caused climate change.

facts.text: Causes include rising seas, more flooding, land turning into wetland, coastal erosion, cyclones, droughts, water shortages and wildfires, which often overlap.
Isle de Jean Charles in Louisiana, about 100 people, became the first total community migration in that state, because of saltwater intrusion and sea level rise.
Vunidogoloa became the first town in Fiji to be depopulated and relocated, after persistent flooding, saltwater intrusion and coastal erosion.
In the Lake Chad Basin, 30,000,000 people are affected by droughts, floods and the lake's shrinking.

title: Beach nourishment

definition.text: Replacing sand lost from a beach through erosion or longshore drift with sediment brought from elsewhere.

facts.text: A wider beach soaks up wave energy across the surf zone, shielding buildings behind it from storm surges and unusually high tides.
It counts as soft engineering: it keeps the beach and avoids the harms of hard structures.
It must be repeated, because it eases the effects of erosion without removing its causes.
The first US project was at Coney Island, New York, in 1922–1923, and the US has spent $9 billion rebuilding beaches since 1923.
The added sand's grain size must closely match the native sand.
New sand can bury bottom-dwelling organisms, disturb seafloor habitat and cut light to nearby reefs and seagrass.
Benefits include higher nearby property values and more tourism, but high erosion rates can make it financially impractical.

definition.text: The loss of land, or long-term removal of sediment and rock, along a coastline by waves, currents, tides, wind-driven water, ice or storms.

facts.text: It works through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and chemical dissolving of rock by seawater.
Softer rock erodes faster than harder rock, carving tunnels, arches and pillars, and over time the coast evens out.
Storms can erode coasts hundreds of times faster than normal weather.
Rising seas let waves reach further inland, speeding shoreline retreat.
It destroys dunes, wetlands, beaches and barrier islands that buffer storms, and it reduces biodiversity.
It damages infrastructure and property, raises protection costs, and harms tourism and fisheries.
Human action can speed it up: Hallsands in Devon was washed away in 1917 after shingle was dredged from its bay.

definition.text: The three common ways to deal with coastal erosion: soft controls, hard controls, and relocation.

facts.text: Hard controls such as seawalls and groynes are more permanent; a seawall lasts about 50–100 years and a groyne 30–40 years.
Soft controls such as sandbags and beach nourishment slow erosion temporarily and are not meant as permanent fixes.
Vegetated 'living shorelines' such as marshes resist storms well; fifteen feet of marsh can absorb fifty percent of incoming wave energy.
Public support for retreat has typically been low.

title: Coastal squeeze

definition.text: The loss of coastal habitat when rising seas push zones such as salt marsh landward and they run up against seawalls or other solid structures.

facts.text: Where sea walls block landward migration and sediment supply is limited, salt marsh cannot keep up with sea level rise.
Wetlands, salt marshes, mangroves and neighbouring freshwater wetlands are especially vulnerable.

notes: No Wikipedia article (page is a Wiktionary redirect); passes the curriculum test by mentions on Managed retreat and Coastal management.

definition.text: Management and rehabilitation of mangrove forests led by local communities, with resource users directly involved.

facts.text: It shifts authority from government to local communities, aiming both to conserve mangroves and to support sustainable livelihoods.
When colonial and post-colonial states took control of mangroves, local people were alienated and the forests were logged and farmed heavily.
Community-managed mangroves show remarkable recovery, and local people have proved effective stewards.
Success depends on communities' willingness to pay and on balancing ecological, economic and social sustainability.

definition.text: A farming system, also called silvofishery, that grows shrimp in ponds alongside planted mangrove trees as a way to rehabilitate mangroves.

facts.text: Expanding shrimp farms are a main cause of mangrove loss, even though shrimp ponds depend on the services mangroves provide.
Like extensive farming, it relies on natural feed and wild shrimp brought in by the tides rather than chemicals and formulated feed, so running costs are low.
Studies in Vietnam found net profit peaks with 30%-50% mangrove cover, while rules requiring 60-80% cover have discouraged farmers.
Benefits include biodiversity, blue carbon storage, coastal protection and steady income, but unequal timber benefit-sharing and conflicting policies hold it back.

definition.text: A dense colony of oysters that builds up into a large reef, also called an oyster bed, bank or bar.

facts.text: New reefs form on stone or hard debris because oyster larvae must settle on hard surfaces; they then grow as young oysters settle on older shells.
Over the last few centuries, overharvesting, lime production and coastal degradation have caused large declines worldwide; 85% of oyster reefs have been removed in two centuries.
Oysters filter phytoplankton and organic matter from the water, buffering estuaries against eutrophication.
Reefs stabilize shorelines by trapping sediment and damping waves, and are recognized as green infrastructure for shoreline protection.
Their nooks shelter prey and young animals, increasing prey biomass.
Restored intertidal eastern oyster reefs can match natural oyster densities and regain stability in about 6 years.

verification.title: Oyster Reefs at Risk and Recommendations for Conservation, Restoration, and Management
verification.evidence: Overall, we estimate that 85% of oyster reefs havebeen lost globally.

definition.text: Restoring marine organisms and ecosystems to their natural state so that damaged seas can recover and thrive on their own.

facts.text: Methods include reintroducing or replenishing species such as oysters, kelp and seagrass.
It can capture carbon, support local economies through ecotourism and reverse biodiversity loss.
Sea rewilding projects are less common than rewilding on land.
More than 90% of the UK's historic seagrass meadows have been lost since the 1930s, and oyster stocks in Europe have fallen 95 per cent.

definition.text: A hard coastal defence built where the sea acts directly on the land, to protect people, property and activities from tides, waves or tsunamis.

facts.text: It works by reflecting wave energy back out to sea, leaving less energy to cause erosion.
Reflected waves can scour and lower the beach in front, and the wall can speed erosion of neighbouring unprotected coasts.
Being static, a seawall clashes with the moving coast and blocks the exchange of sediment between land and sea.
High costs and environmental side effects have led to more use of soft options such as beach replenishment.
Rising seas raise both normal water levels and storm wave heights, which existing walls may not withstand.
At least 43 percent of Japan's coastline is lined with seawalls or similar structures, yet in 2011 the tsunami overwhelmed seawalls in most areas.
A cost-benefit approach helps decide whether a seawall is worth its expense.

definition.text: Coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, coral reefs and coastal vegetation that blunt tsunamis and storm surges like a living seawall.

facts.text: A UNEP report found the 26 December 2004 tsunami did less damage where mangroves, coral reefs or coastal vegetation were present.
Weeks after that disaster, India began planting Casuarina and coconut saplings along its coast as a natural barrier.
Reefs can damp waves as well as or better than artificial breakwaters.

definition.text: A shoreline management practice that uses ecological principles and natural materials to stabilize shorelines and protect waterside habitats.

facts.text: It places vegetation, stones, sand, logs and similar materials to reduce erosion, soften the land-water edge and lower restoration costs.
Its guiding principles are to imitate nature, use gentle slopes that spread wave energy, use living 'soft armour', and mix materials for biodiversity.
The most basic technique is planting native vegetation whose roots bind the soil.
Other tools include coir logs, live stakes and fascines, brush mattresses, live cribwalls and vegetated riprap.
Coastal engineering shifted gradually toward including the natural environment late in the 20th century.
Soft and hard engineering can be blended, especially on fast-flowing waters.
Around the Detroit River, 38 soft engineering projects cost $17.3 million and showed strong economic and social benefits.

title: Hard engineering

definition.text: Protecting shorelines with non-living reinforcing materials such as concrete, steel and rock to stop erosion and flooding.

facts.text: The four main hard structures in coastal engineering are the seawall, revetment, groyne and breakwater.
Hard shoreline engineering mainly serves navigation, industry and commerce.
It destroyed biological communities, cut off waterside habitats and disrupted natural sediment movement; the Detroit River lost as much as 97% of its coastal wetlands.
Each hard structure gives only temporary protection and creates an end effect that erodes neighbouring coasts.

notes: No article of its own; defined on Soft engineering and mentioned on Seawall, Beach nourishment, Sand dune stabilization and Floodplain restoration.
